Self-probe (the typical case, country of birth switched from the United States to Portugal): this part's contribution (its exit minus the exit's training mean) moves from 0.00 to -1.98 on the log-odds scale and the predicted chance from 71% to 35%. The step is fitted to 49 Portuguese-born training rows, and it is not borne out by them: their observed rate of a low income is 81.6% against a mean predicted chance of 75.1%. Switching the part off leaves the training AUC at 0.9099 (with it, 0.9099).
ann_126.proposed: Birth in Portugal lowers the predicted chance of a low income by a large fixed step, for a typical person from about 71% to about 25%.

ann_127.original: Prediction: the more education, the lower the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 a year or less). The part is a sum of direct edges (formula attached): the education level scale has weight -0.98 per sd, and six level indicators add smaller terms. Self-probe (the typical case with matching education and education level set): the predicted chance is 84% for 11th grade (education=1), 71% for high-school graduate (education=11), 62% for some college (education=15), 42% for bachelor's degree (education=9), 34% for master's degree (education=12) and 14% for doctorate (education=10), falling at each step. Removing the education level edge alone lowers the training AUC from 0.9099 to 0.8796; switching off the whole part, to 0.8924.
ann_127.proposed: More education lowers the predicted chance of a low income: for a typical person, about 34% with a master's degree and about 42% with a bachelor's degree, against about 71% for a high-school graduate.

ann_128.original: Prediction: longer working hours and capital losses lower the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 a year or less); executive or managerial work lowers it and manual or farm work raises it. The part is a sum of direct edges (formula attached): hours worked per week -0.29 and capital losses -0.28 per sd, with smaller terms for work class, occupation indicators and the census sampling weight. Self-probe (the typical case, hours swept): the predicted chance is 79% at 20 hours, 71% at 40 hours and 60% at 60 hours. With occupation set instead, this part's contribution (its exit minus the exit's training mean) is -0.03 for a professional specialty, -0.45 for executive or managerial work, 0.66 for a machine operator and 1.20 for farming or fishing (log-odds). 1820 training people report a capital loss; their observed rate of a low income is 49.4%. Switching the part off lowers the training AUC from 0.9099 to 0.8981.
ann_128.proposed: Through this part, capital losses and longer working hours lower the predicted chance of a low income steadily, and the kind of job and work class move it by fixed steps.

ann_129.original: Prediction: being married to a civilian spouse lowers the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 a year or less), and men get a lower predicted chance than women. The part is a sum of direct edges (formula attached): married to a civilian spouse -0.70 and sex (male) -0.25 per sd, with small terms for two other marital statuses and two race levels. Self-probe (the typical case with marital status and sex set): this part's contribution (its exit minus the exit's training mean) is -0.94 for a married man, -0.41 for a married woman, 0.48 for a never-married man and 1.00 for a never-married woman (log-odds); with the relationship held at husband, so for constructed cases, the whole-model predicted chances are 71%, 80%, 91% and 94%. Switching the part off lowers the training AUC from 0.9099 to 0.8901.
ann_129.proposed: Through this part, a typical woman (never married, not in a family) gets about 94% against about 71% for a husband, and marital statuses other than married raise it to about 91%.

ann_130.original: Prediction: people born outside the United States, in a country without a term of its own, get a higher predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 a year or less) than people born in the United States. The part is a sum of direct edges on country indicators (formula attached); the United States indicator carries -0.14 per sd, and because most people are US-born (35123 of 39073), being off it moves the score up. Self-probe (the typical case, country of birth set): this part's contribution (its exit minus the exit's training mean) is -0.03 for the United States and 0.44 for Mexico (log-odds), and the predicted chance 71% and 79%. The largest country weight, on the Netherlands, never acts on a training row: 0 training people were born in the Netherlands. Switching the part off changes the training AUC from 0.9099 to 0.9095.
ann_130.proposed: Each country of birth with a term of its own moves the predicted chance of a low income by a fixed amount compared with the United States, for example down to about 46% for Ireland and up to about 94% for Trinidad and Tobago.

ann_132.original: Prediction: married people, wives and husbands, get the lowest predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 a year or less) from the household terms, and people living as a child of the household the highest. The junction (identity node) adds the exits of relationship_chain, handlers_not_in_family and direct_personal with weight one, on the log-odds scale. Self-probe (the typical case with relationship, marital status and sex set together): the part's contribution (its exit minus the exit's training mean) is -1.94 for a married wife, -1.53 for a married husband, 0.56 for a never-married man not in a family, 1.40 for an unmarried divorced woman and 1.59 for a never-married man living as a child of the household (log-odds); the whole-model predicted chances are 61%, 71%, 95%, 98% and 98%. This is the largest part: switching it off lowers the training AUC from 0.9099 to 0.8465.
ann_132.proposed: The household terms add up: for a typical person, a husband gets about 71%, a woman (never married, not in a family) about 97% and an unmarried person (so divorced) about 96%; the rises are smaller for handlers or cleaners, who start higher.

ann_133.original: Prediction: the model is additive on the log-odds scale: the output adds the exits of its eight children and applies a sigmoid; each part's exit depends on its own inputs alone, so a change in one part's inputs moves the score by an amount that does not depend on the inputs of the other parts, while the shift in predicted chance is largest where that chance is near the middle of its range. Self-probe (the typical case, capital gains and age set): capital gains of 5000 US dollars instead of 0 US dollars move the score from 1.32 to -0.37 at 30 years and from 0.08 to -1.61 at 50 years, steps of equal size, while the predicted chance moves from 79% to 41% and from 52% to 17%. The typical training case is aged 37 years, a husband married to a civilian spouse, a high-school graduate in a professional specialty working 40 hours a week with no capital gains, born in the United States; the model gives this person 71%. Over the training split the mean predicted chance is 75.7% against an observed rate of 76.1%, and the training AUC is 0.9099. By AUC loss when switched off, the largest parts are household (AUC to 0.8465), relationship_chain (to 0.8873) and direct_personal (to 0.8901); the hidden units add an age hinge, a Colombia regime fitted to 64 rows, a Portugal step fitted to 49 rows and fixed shifts for a few occupation and household categories, and the rest of the model is direct edges. In the probes of this explanation, a part's contribution is its exit minus the exit's training mean (the score change when it is switched off), except for the gated missing_records part, whose contribution is its exit itself.
ann_133.proposed: The model adds up the scores of eight parts (capital gains, the household, age, education, work, missing records, country of birth and Portugal); a typical person, a 37-year-old husband who finished high school, gets a predicted chance of a low income of about 71%.

Self-probe (the typical case, capital gains and age set): capital gains of 5000 US dollars instead of 0 US dollars move the score from 1.32 to -0.37 at 30 years and from 0.08 to -1.61 at 50 years, steps of equal size, while the predicted chance moves from 79% to 41% and from 52% to 17%. The typical training case is aged 37 years, a husband married to a civilian spouse, a high-school graduate in a professional specialty working 40 hours a week with no capital gains, born in the United States; the model gives this person 71%. Over the training split the mean predicted chance is 75.7% against an observed rate of 76.1%, and the training AUC is 0.9099. By AUC loss when switched off, the largest parts are household (AUC to 0.8465), relationship_chain (to 0.8873) and direct_personal (to 0.8901); the hidden units add an age hinge, a Colombia regime fitted to 64 rows, a Portugal step fitted to 49 rows and fixed shifts for a few occupation and household categories, and the rest of the model is direct edges.
